article.overview: A sample return capsule is the re-entry vehicle, or the part of a spacecraft, that carries returned extraterrestrial material through the atmosphere and delivers it to the ground in a sealed, protected container. For a lunar mission, the capsule is the last link in a chain that begins on the Moon with collection and sealing and ends in a curation laboratory on Earth.
article.description: Sample return capsules are usually small, heavily protected vehicles. They must survive the heating and deceleration of atmospheric entry, reach the ground at a controlled speed, and keep the returned material intact and uncontaminated. Their designs typically combine a heat shield on the leading face, a sealed sample container, a parachute or other recovery system, and a means of locating the capsule after landing. Some capsules are released from a larger spacecraft shortly before entry, while others are part of a crewed return vehicle. The term 'sample return capsule' describes a function rather than one design. Lunar sample return capsules have been flown by the Soviet Union (Luna 16, Luna 20 and Luna 24) and by China (Chang'e-5). The Apollo missions returned lunar samples inside the crewed Apollo spacecraft rather than in a separate capsule. Non-lunar sample return capsules, such as those from OSIRIS-REx (asteroid Bennu) and Hayabusa2 (asteroid Ryugu), are included as engineering analogues. They are not lunar payloads.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a sample return capsule is to bring material collected in space back to laboratories where it can be analysed with instruments that are too large, too heavy or too sensitive to fly. Returned lunar samples allow researchers to measure isotopic ages, chemical composition, mineralogy, volatile content and the physical properties of regolith and rock. Such measurements constrain the Moon's geological history, the timing of volcanic and impact events, and the processes that have shaped the surface. Returned samples also provide ground truth for remote-sensing data and for orbital and surface instruments, because a sample has a known location and context. The Luna and Apollo sample programmes are the main historical examples of this. The Chang'e-5 return added a further lunar sample set, although the sources reviewed for this article did not give enough detail on its geological context to describe it. Sample return also supports preservation and curation: returned material can be stored, subdivided, shared between institutions and re-examined as analytical methods improve. This is one reason the containment and sealing of the capsule matter as much as the re-entry system.
article.operating_principle: A sample return capsule operates in several phases. (1) Sample collection and sealing: material is gathered on the Moon, in a small body, or by a sampler, and placed in a container that is sealed, often in a controlled environment, to limit loss of volatiles and contamination. (2) Transfer into the capsule: the sealed container is moved into the capsule, or the capsule is the container itself; the OSIRIS-REx sample canister was removed and processed only after the capsule reached the curation facility. (3) Separation and transit: for spacecraft that release a capsule, the capsule separates from the main vehicle before atmospheric entry; the Chang'e-5 return capsule separated about 5,000 km from Earth before entering the atmosphere. (4) Atmospheric entry: a heat shield absorbs and dissipates the heat generated by friction with the atmosphere. Some missions use a skip (bounce) re-entry, in which the vehicle first grazes the upper atmosphere before descending; Chang'e-5 used a skip re-entry profile. (5) Descent and recovery: a parachute system reduces the speed, and the capsule is located and recovered, typically by ground teams or, in the OSIRIS-REx case, with helicopter support. (6) Handling and curation: the sealed container is transported to a laboratory where it is opened under controlled conditions and the material is catalogued.
article.scientific_importance: Sample return is one of the few ways to obtain material from another body and analyse it with laboratory instruments that cannot be flown on a robotic lander. Lunar samples have shaped the understanding of the Moon's age, formation and early history, and returned asteroid samples (OSIRIS-REx and Hayabusa2) have been used for similar analyses of primitive small bodies. The Soviet Luna programme returned lunar soil in the 1970s, and the Apollo programme returned substantially larger amounts. More recently, the Chang'e-5 return added a further lunar sample set. Each returned set is scientifically valuable because the sample set is finite and the analysis is repeatable only when the material has been preserved well.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power requirement for a sample return capsule. Sample quantity, heat-shield requirements, the return trajectory and the recovery method all change the design. The values below describe specific missions and should not be generalised. Where a value is not publicly specified or was not verified, the entry says so. Unlike-for-unlike comparisons are avoided: the lunar and non-lunar examples differ in entry speed, heat-shield design, sample quantity and mission architecture.

examples.name: Soviet Luna 16, Luna 20 and Luna 24 return capsules
examples.sample_mass_notes: Sample masses are from secondary sources (Wikipedia mirrors and historical sites). Some tables give 30 g for Luna 20, which was not resolved. Luna 24 core length is inconsistent across sources (about 1.6 m to 2.5 m reported), so no single core length is stated.
examples.sampling_method: Luna 16 and Luna 20 collected soil from a depth of a few tens of centimetres. Luna 24 was designed to drill deeper.
examples.landing_and_return_notes: Luna 24 launched on 9 August 1976; its return capsule parachuted down on 22 August 1976 about 200 km south-east of Surgut in western Siberia (secondary sources). Luna 16 landed in Mare Fecunditatis, Luna 20 in highlands between Fecunditatis and Crisium, and Luna 24 in Mare Crisium.
examples.qualification: Capsule dimensions and capsule mass were not verified. These are historical examples; no current design specification is implied.

examples.name: Chang'e-5 return capsule
examples.flight_status: Flown: landed 16 December 2020 at 17:59 GMT (about 01:59 on 17 December Beijing time) at Siziwang Banner, Inner Mongolia
examples.mass_qualifier: Approximate. The ESA eoportal page gives '~300 kg' in a figure caption. Single-source figure; not checked against CNSA or a primary mission paper.

external_dimensions_cm.qualifier: Secondary source only (SpacePolicyOnline reports about 1 m in diameter and about 1 m high). Not confirmed against a CNSA or primary publication. The eoportal page gives no capsule dimensions.

examples.sample_returned_note: Measured sample mass given on the ESA eoportal page. The original target was about 2 kg.
examples.entry_and_recovery: Capsule separated about 5,000 km from Earth before entering the atmosphere. It performed a skip re-entry, used a drogue parachute followed by a main parachute, and landed at Siziwang Banner, Inner Mongolia.
examples.whole_spacecraft_note: Whole-stack figure for the full Chang'e-5 spacecraft (all four modules). Not the return capsule mass.
examples.qualification: The return capsule mass is approximate. The sample mass is a measured figure. Dimensions are secondary-source only.

examples.name: Apollo sample containers and Lunar Receiving Laboratory
examples.type: Historical containment and curation chain (not a dedicated sample return capsule)
examples.flight_status: Flown: Apollo lunar surface missions with sample return via the crewed Apollo spacecraft (Apollo 11, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 17; Apollo 13 did not land)
examples.containment_notes: Sealed containers were sterilised on the outside before being moved in or out of the high-vacuum complex at the Lunar Receiving Laboratory (LRL), Houston. The LRL high-vacuum complex was used for Apollo 11 and 12 sample processing and was deactivated in November 1970 after Apollo 13. Later missions were handled more as curation than quarantine work.
examples.quarantine_statistics: About 2 per cent of the Apollo 11, 12 and 14 sample mass (1.990 kg of 98.189 kg) went to quarantine biological testing, per a NASA report reviewed through a search excerpt only.
examples.qualification: No verified mass, dimension or power figure for the Apollo sample containers was found. Statements are from NASA reports reviewed through search excerpts; the full PDFs were not read.

examples.name: OSIRIS-REx sample return capsule
examples.type: Flown non-lunar sample return capsule (asteroid 101955 Bennu); engineering analogue, not a lunar payload
examples.flight_status: Flown: landed 24 September 2023 at the Utah Test and Training Range
examples.mass_qualifier: Approximately 46 kg (100 lb). Figure from a NASA press kit excerpt seen through a search result, and from Spaceflight101 (secondary). The NASA press kit PDF was not readable in full.

external_dimensions_cm.qualifier: Spaceflight101 (secondary); blunt-nosed cone. No official NASA figure for the diameter was found in this review.

examples.heat_shield: Phenolic-impregnated carbon ablator (PICA), a material developed at NASA Ames (secondary source). Heritage: described as nearly identical to the Stardust sample return capsule (secondary source).
examples.sample_returned_note: NASA mission milestone: 4.29 ounces (121.6 g) of Bennu material delivered on return.
examples.entry_and_recovery: Capsule parachuted to the Department of Defense's Utah Test and Training Range, where the OSIRIS-REx team retrieved it. Helicopter transport to the cleanroom followed landing.
examples.entry_speed_and_heating: Secondary source: about 27,000 mph entry speed and heating to about 5,000 degrees Fahrenheit. Not confirmed against a primary NASA document.
examples.qualification: Diameter from Spaceflight101 (secondary). Mass from a NASA press kit excerpt and Spaceflight101. Sample mass from the NASA mission milestones page.

examples.name: Hayabusa2 sample return capsule
examples.type: Flown non-lunar sample return capsule (asteroid Ryugu); engineering analogue, not a lunar payload
examples.flight_status: Flown: sent back on 5 December 2020; recovered on 6 December 2020 in Australia (JAXA)
examples.mass_qualifier: From a DLR image caption ('weighs 16 kilograms').

external_dimensions_cm.qualifier: Height from the DLR caption. Diameter not verified in a primary source; a secondary source gives 40 cm, which was not used.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The examples differ greatly. The Chang'e-5 capsule is reported as about 1 m in diameter and 1 m high (secondary source). The OSIRIS-REx capsule is reported as a blunt-nosed cone about 81 cm in diameter and 50 cm tall (secondary source). The Hayabusa2 capsule is reported as 40 cm high (DLR). The Luna capsule dimensions were not verified. Dimensions for a new capsule would depend on the sample quantity, the heat-shield design and the containment approach, none of which can be inferred from these examples.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Verified or reported capsule masses are: Chang'e-5 about 300 kg (approximate, single-source); OSIRIS-REx about 46 kg (press kit excerpt and secondary source); Hayabusa2 about 16 kg (DLR). Luna capsule masses were not verified. Apollo container masses were not verified. Whole-spacecraft masses (for example Chang'e-5 about 8,200 kg launch mass and Hayabusa2 about 600 kg) are not capsule masses and should not be used for capsule comparisons.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified for the capsules reviewed. Sample return capsules are generally passive during transit and re-entry, and the reviewed sources did not describe a capsule power system in detail.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A sample return capsule must work across several environments. On the lunar surface and during collection, the sample is exposed to a vacuum, large temperature swings and dust; the container must limit loss of volatiles and contamination during handling and sealing. During transit, the capsule must survive the thermal and radiation environment of the space journey. During atmospheric entry, the heat shield must withstand high heating loads (the OSIRIS-REx entry heating figure is secondary-source only). Operationally, the capsule must land within a recoverable area, be found quickly and be transported in a manner that protects the sample. The OSIRIS-REx capsule was transported by helicopter to a cleanroom, then disassembled and packaged for shipment to NASA's Johnson Space Center, where the sample canister lid was removed on 26 September 2023, according to the NASA mission milestones page.
article.limitations: A sample return capsule is a single-use system. It cannot be tested in its flight environment on Earth, so it depends on ground testing, analysis and flight heritage. Some key values for lunar capsules (for example, Luna capsule dimensions and mass, and the Apollo containers' mass) were not verified in this review. Sample quantity is a strong constraint, and the scientific value of a sample depends on its documented context. Containment and contamination control are also limitations: the Apollo quarantine and curation experience showed that negative-pressure containment alone did not solve the contamination problem, and that a balance between containment and cleanliness is required.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A sample return capsule is not normally deployed on the lunar surface. Its transportation chain differs from that of a surface payload: containment and sealing on the Moon, transfer to a return vehicle, lunar departure, separation, entry, descent, recovery and transport to a curation facility.
transportation_process: Containment and sealing on the Moon: the sample is collected and placed in a sealed container. The ascent-stage arrangements used to lift samples off the surface or into lunar orbit were not described in detail in the sources reviewed.

Transfer to the return vehicle: according to the ESA eoportal page, the Chang'e-5 ascender docked on 6 December 2020 and transferred the samples. The reviewed excerpt does not name the receiving module in detail. The ascender was then crashed into the Moon on 8 December 2020, per the same page.

Lunar departure and separation: the Chang'e-5 orbiter and return capsule left lunar orbit together on 12 December 2020, and the capsule separated about 5,000 km from Earth on 16 December 2020 (eoportal).
Entry, descent and recovery: the Chang'e-5 capsule performed a skip re-entry and landed at Siziwang Banner, Inner Mongolia, on 16 December 2020 (17:59 GMT, eoportal).

Transport to a curation facility: returned capsules are transported to laboratories under controlled conditions. The OSIRIS-REx capsule arrived at NASA's Johnson Space Center on 25 September 2023, the day after landing, according to the NASA mission milestones page.
Sample handling after arrival: the OSIRIS-REx sample canister lid was removed on 26 September 2023, the start of curation, per the NASA mission milestones page.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Not applicable in the usual surface-deployment sense. Sample return capsules are recovered after Earth entry rather than deployed on the lunar surface. The OSIRIS-REx capsule was recovered by ground team and helicopter transfer after its Utah landing.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Luna 16, Luna 20 and Luna 24 capsules returned lunar soil in 1970, 1972 and 1976. The Chang'e-5 capsule returned lunar samples in December 2020. The Apollo missions returned lunar samples through the crewed spacecraft and the Lunar Receiving Laboratory. The OSIRIS-REx and Hayabusa2 capsules returned asteroid samples in 2023 and 2020 respectively; these are non-lunar analogues.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility is asserted between a sample return capsule and any named lunar lander or spacecraft. A lunar sample return capsule would need its mass, dimensions, interface loads, power and data requirements, and containment requirements checked against verified spacecraft specifications before any compatibility assessment could be made. The Chang'e-5 and Luna systems are examples of integrated return architectures, not interface references for another vehicle.

article.historical_significance: The Luna programme (1970 to 1976) demonstrated that robotic spacecraft could return lunar soil from the Moon; Luna 16 (1970) was the first robotic lunar sample return. The Apollo missions returned substantially more lunar material and established the curation and quarantine practices that later became the basis for NASA's astromaterials curation. Chang'e-5 (2020) was described in press accounts reviewed for this article as the first lunar sample return since 1976. The OSIRIS-REx and Hayabusa2 missions returned asteroid samples in 2023 and 2020, demonstrating sample return technology in non-lunar settings.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The term 'sample return capsule' describes a class of vehicles rather than one standard design. The Luna, Chang'e-5, OSIRIS-REx and Hayabusa2 capsules are not interchangeable. The Chang'e-5 capsule dimensions (about 1 m in diameter and 1 m high) come from a secondary source and have not been checked against a CNSA or primary publication. The Luna sample masses come from secondary sources, and the Luna 20 and Luna 24 values are not consistent across sources; the Luna 24 core length is not resolved. The OSIRIS-REx capsule dimensions and mass come from Spaceflight101 and a NASA press kit excerpt; the NASA press kit and factsheet PDFs were not readable in full. The Apollo laboratory statements come from NASA reports reviewed only through search excerpts. No verified lunar lander compatibility, landing-site recommendation or future-capsule lunar payload mass is given; lunar location recommendations are deferred by the user.

data_quality_notes: Catalogue check: ID 259, name 'Sample return capsule' and category 13 'Sample collection, preservation and return' match lunar_payloads_catalogue_320.md.

Research was limited to 9 standard-mode web searches plus fetches. Extended-mode search was not used. Several facts rest on secondary sources (Wikipedia mirrors, Spaceflight101, SpacePolicyOnline, Astronomy.com) and are marked in references and examples.

Chang'e-5 return capsule mass (about 300 kg) is an approximate single-source figure from the ESA eoportal page. Capsule dimensions (about 1 m diameter and 1 m high) come from SpacePolicyOnline only and are unconfirmed.

Luna 16, Luna 20 and Luna 24 sample masses (101 g, 55 g, 170 g) come from secondary sources. Luna 20 also appears as 30 g in some sources. Luna 24 core length conflicts across sources (about 1.6 m to 2.5 m; 2 m and 160 cm also reported). Luna capsule dimensions and mass were not verified.

Apollo sample-container and Lunar Receiving Laboratory statements come from NASA NTRS reports reviewed only through search excerpts; the PDFs were not read in full. No Apollo container mass, dimension or power value was verified.

OSIRIS-REx capsule diameter (81 cm) and height (50 cm) come from Spaceflight101 only; the NASA press kit mass (100 lb, 46 kg) was seen through a search excerpt. The NASA press kit PDF and NASA factsheet PDF (osiris_rex_factsheet5-25.pdf) returned binary content and were not readable. The Spaceflight101 capsule sub-page was reached via ?p=281; the clean URL https://spaceflight101.com/osiris-rex/ should be checked before publication.
OSIRIS-REx entry speed (about 27,000 mph) and heating (about 5,000 degrees F) are from a secondary source and were not confirmed against a NASA primary document.

Hayabusa2 capsule height (40 cm) and mass (16 kg) are from a DLR image caption. Capsule diameter was not verified in a primary source. JAXA page gives whole-spacecraft mass (about 600 kg) without stating launch or dry mass.
Power consumption and power requirements for all capsules were not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

Image verification: the single included image (NASA/Keegan Barber, NHQ202309240011) was checked by HTTP HEAD (image/jpeg, HTTP 200) and its source page returned HTTP 200 on 2026-11-13. Full-resolution download was not checked. No other direct image URL was verified, so no other images are included.
The Hayabusa2 DLR image shows a model of the 2010 Hayabusa capsule and is not used in this article as a Hayabusa2 image; its CC BY-SA 3.0 licence was noted by the source but not used.
Canonical Wikipedia URLs for Luna 16, Luna 20 and Luna 24 were cited based on mirror pages seen in search results; the canonical pages were not fetched.
Chang'e-5 landing and separation dates and times (16 December 2020 at 17:59 GMT) are from the eoportal page; press accounts vary in local-time reporting (about 01:59 on 17 December Beijing time).
No lunar landing-site recommendation, lander compatibility or future-capsule lunar mass is asserted. Lunar location recommendations are deferred by the user.
No person is named in the article, so no pronoun assumptions were needed.
